newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat to ask Clinton to put pressure on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arafat to ask Clinton to put pressure on Israel.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat begins an official visit to the United States on Sunday amid rising tension over Israel's decision to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

During a scheduled Monday morning meeting at the White House, Arafat hopes to persuade U.S. President Bill Clinton to press Israel to reverse the decision to build 6,500 homes for Jews at Jabal Abu Ghneim, known by Israelis as Har Homa, PLO officials said.

Arafat, who left Egypt for the United States early on Sunday, told the Cairo-based Arab League on Saturday the Israeli plan was an attempt to destroy the peace process and said peace with settlements was impossible.
He suggested he might retaliate by declaring a Palestinian state, a gesture likely to anger right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"We are supposed to declare the setting up of a Palestinian state in five years, but what would happen if I declare it right here? What would he (Netanyahu) do then? It's tit-for-tat and we have our weapons too," he said.

Arafat's adviser, Marwan Kanafani, told Reuters earlier: "This visit is important politically because we have to find a way out of the impasse caused by Israel's decision to build homes for Jews on Jabal Abu Ghneim,"
Arafat was also expected to raise the issue at talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright later on Monday.

The White House has said the decision "further complicates an already complicated situation", but has also sounded a warning against any attempt by Palestinians to express their grievances through violence.

Last September, Palestinian anger over Israel's decision to open a tourist tunnel in Arab East Jerusalem near Moslem holy sites sparked gun battles in which 61 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died.

Arafat will go to New York on Tuesday evening to confer with U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and hold other meetings before flying to Houston, Texas, on Wednesday for talks with former U.S. president George Bush. From there he goes to Europe.
Kanafani said Arafat would seek "tangible American measures to ensure that the peace process continues in a meaningful way".
Analysts said Arafat needed U.S. political and economic backing to deflate mounting tension among Palestinians over the planned building.
Palestinians have charged that Israel was trying to pre-empt a decision on the final status of Jerusalem, which is supposed to be decided in future talks that must be completed in 1999.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and views all of the city as its capital. Palestinians want Arab East Jerusalem to be the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Palestinians said the housing project could spark anti-Israeli violence in the West Bank and Gaza reminiscent of last year's clashes that almost wrecked the Israeli-PLO peace process.

"What the Israeli government is doing here at Jabal Abu Ghneim and other places...can destroy everything," said Faisal al-Husseini, the top PLO official in Jerusalem, after Israel's decision last Wednesday. "Everything is ready for an explosion."
